title: Four entered the orchard
hookLine: traditionally for the mature and learned; today many study it with a teacher
carry: mystical study needs solid ground and a teacher

lines: A RULE LIKE A SIGN ON A DOOR.
NOT TO TWO. NOT EVEN TO ONE.
cards: There's a rule in the Mishnah that reads like a sign on a door. Some subjects, it says, are not to be taught in a crowd. The account of creation, not to two at once.
The chariot that Ezekiel saw, not even to one, unless that one is already wise and understands on their own. The rest of the Torah carries no such sign.
Tradition kept the mystical teachings for people who were mature and already learned. Today, people study them in classes and books, often with a teacher beside them.

teach.b: Enter carefully. The Talmud tells a short, strange story about why.
Four sages, it says, entered the pardes, the orchard; some readers hear it as the hidden depths of the Torah. Ben Azzai looked, and died. Ben Zoma looked, and was harmed.
Elisha ben Abuyah, whom the Talmud calls Acher, the other one, cut down the shoots, which readers take to mean he left the path.
Only Rabbi Akiva, the story says, entered in peace and went out in peace. First, the orchard is real enough to hurt. The story doesn't say mystical study is bad.
It says it's strong, and strength needs care. Second, look at who walks out whole. The story doesn't say why it was Akiva.
Some readers point to what else the Talmud tells of him: a teacher of the law, surrounded by students, steeped in the plain sense of the text.
On that reading, the ground you stand on before you go in counts for a great deal. Third, the door isn't locked forever.
The same tradition that warns at the doorway also kept the teachings, copied them and handed them down. Caution was a way of protecting them, not burying them. Fourth, the teacher.
The Mishnah's picture is a sage beside one student, not a stranger with a book: someone who has been in the orchard and can say, slow down, look here, not yet.
So entering carefully is less about fear than about humility: knowing you're a guest in a very old garden.

how: Jewish mystical texts have traditionally been studied by people already grounded in Torah and Talmud; today they are also taught in classes and study circles, usually with a teacher guiding the reading.

o: study the secrets alone so no one leads you astray
go slowly, on solid learning, with a teacher beside you
stay away from mystical study for your whole life

games.q: the four who entered — tap the pairs.
p: in peace, and out in peace

s: the story of the orchard says mystical study is bad
it says the orchard is strong. one sage walks in and out whole.
the Mishnah limits how some subjects are taught
the account of creation and the chariot are not taught openly, in a crowd.
the one who comes out whole is the boldest of the four
it's Rabbi Akiva, whose life stood on ordinary learning and teaching.

games.q: you're one of four sages walking into the orchard of hidden teachings. what does the story say carries you out whole?
games.why: only Rabbi Akiva entered in peace and went out in peace, the story says: the one who already knew the ground.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you want to understand but don't yet, a text, a skill, a person, a question about God, and say to yourself quietly: I don't know this yet.
Notice how it feels to stand at the door instead of pushing through it. Then hold the name of one person who could walk you in, a teacher, a friend, or someone who writes carefully.

wordCard.voice: Enter carefully. The tradition's advice at the door of mystical study: go slowly, stand on solid learning, and walk in with a teacher. Today's words.

orig.note: Hebrew: an orchard, the garden the four sages entered in the Talmud's story.

carryVoice: Your line: mystical study needs solid ground and a teacher. A guest in an old garden walks slowly. Go gently.
